quotes.quote: Test Writing consists of 90 high quality tasks that target a coding agent's Test Writing ability.
The benchmark consists of tasks drawn from 11 production repositories across 4 programming languages - Go, Python, C, and TypeScript.
An LLM judge (Claude Opus 4.5) checks if the manifest accurately lists all the changes made by the agent
Pass criteria: All tests listed in the manifest pass and all tests must fail after mutation i.e. no extraneous tests are added
Pass criteria: All must-have rubrics are graded as a Pass.
We use mandatory rubrics (Test Comprehensiveness) to score and rank the models. The grading of the nice-to-have rubrics are used only for qualitative analysis.
Each model was run with 3 trials, and we report the mean resolve rate across the trials.
Top models score under 45%, with a substantial room for improvement.
The biggest failure mode is rubrics – models often miss writing tests that are expected for the behavior described, thus failing one or more mandatory rubrics.
Models have a higher mutation fail rate – they sometimes write tests that are extraneous and do not test the behavior described in the prompt.

Interestingly, the scaffold makes a lot of difference here, where Anthropic and OpenAI's model scores being significantly better (+10% absolute difference) in test placement and logical consistency when they are run on their native scaffold instead of mini-swe-agent.

GPT 5.4's ability to perform deep exploration of the codebase, active runtime analysis and tendency to write precise tests that target the given behavior in the prompt contribute to its high performance.
There is also a strong positive correlation between models that write a lot of tests, and their mutation failure rate.

We have updated the dataset to prevent solution lookup opportunities, since we observed that frontier models like Fable 5 and GPT 5.6 started looking up the upstream fixes using curl, git and in some cases, source files from the packages when it cant use the local git commits.
We have increased mini-swe-agent step count from 250 to 500 for newer models like Muse Spark, GLM 5.2 and will continue to use that, to allow more room for exploration.
For Fable-5 (Claude Code) xHigh we observed an elevated refusal rate on this benchmark when we ran this model, since it triggered security related filters.

We introduce SWE Atlas, a benchmark suite for coding agents spanning three professional software engineering workflows: Codebase Q&A (124 tasks), Test Writing (90 tasks), and Refactoring (70 tasks).
A new benchmark of 284 expert-authored SWE tasks spanning Codebase Q&A (124), Test Writing (90), and Refactoring (70), drawn from 18 actively maintained open-source repositories.
Pass criteria: Manifest check pass and mutation test pass and rubrics (all mandatory rubric items).
The check passes if the agent's tests pass in the first run and fail or error out in the second, since the tests should fail when the relevant code is broken.

Only Test Comprehensiveness rubrics are must-have; the rest produce qualitative signal that helps us evaluate the responses with a professional SWE standard, but are not used to grade the correctness for final score.
We source professional software engineers with several years of experience working on real-world software engineering to create this benchmark.
Finally, all tasks are audited by three trusted experts independently, to check the instructions, verification setup and rubrics.
We filter out rubrics that were marked as invalid, over-prescriptive or ambiguous by at least 2 of the 3 experts.
All tasks have a single user turn, and we leave multi-turn tasks as future work.
Following SWE-Bench Pro [9], we use high-quality actively maintained open-source repositories as the environments for creating tasks.

we run the best models on their provider's first-party harness (Codex CLI for OpenAI, Claude Code for Anthropic, Gemini CLI for Google) to reproduce end-user experience and elicit the best performance on the benchmark
In addition, we use mini-SWE-agent, which uses just the bash command as a tool for the agent, as a minimal harness to evaluate some models under a common scaffold.

Table 1: Resolution rates on SWE Atlas, averaged over 3 trials. Pass@1 is the mean per-trial pass rate (Wilson 95% CI computed at the trial level); Pass3 is the fraction of tasks where all three trials pass (consistency).
even the best configurations drop by 30-50% from Pass@1 to Pass3 , indicating that models do not consistently produce correct answers across trials
Most models excel at writing good manifests.
The key differentiator is rubric check and mutation check.
we found a recurring pattern: agents write comprehensive tests but with weak assertions, so the test passes on the broken mutant code just as it does on the original.
Test Writing tasks are partitioned by test scope — Integration Tests, Unit Tests, and Acceptance Tests.
On Test Writing, all models excel relatively at Unit and Integration tests but perform poorly on Acceptance tests.
We observe that cost per task increases as the pass rate increases.
